name: Mustardé otoplasty

lead: Mustardé otoplasty sets back prominent ears. Permanent mattress stitches create or deepen the antihelical fold, so the rim sits closer to the head, and the cartilage is not cut. The pinned-back ear is visible once healed.

It dates to J. C. Mustardé's 1963 paper and is commonly used for prominent ear deformity. A retrospective study of patients under 18 characterised it as a good-fast-cheap technique when assessed for quality, time and cost. Published support is mostly retrospective series and technique descriptions, and in looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxx ear procedure.

paras: It is an open method: the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, a strip of skin is removed, and mattress sutures fold the antihelix. It is often paired with Furnas sutures for ears with a deep bowl. A surgeon performs it, usually in a single short operation.
Documented complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion with granulomas, scarring, and overcorrection or an unnatural contour.

angle.text: Stitches fold the ear cartilage into a natural antihelical fold, setting prominent ears closer to the head without cutting the cartilage. The pinned-back ear is visible once healed. It is a long-established technique supported mostly by retrospective series.

lead: Mustardé otoplasty is a technique for correcting prominent ears. Permanent mattress sutures are placed to create or deepen the antihelical fold, which brings the helical rim closer to the side of the head, without cutting through the cartilage [1]. For people who dislike how far their ears stand out, the result is a flatter, more proportioned ear profile and a cleaner silhouette of the head from the front and back. It rests on J. C. Mustardé's 1963 paper on correcting prominent ears with simple mattress sutures [1].

A general reference classes it among the techniques that keep the ear cartilage intact, describing it as an open method in which the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, a strip of skin removed and mattress sutures placed [1]. It is described as commonly used for prominent ear deformity [2], and a retrospective study of patients under 18 characterised it as a "good-fast-cheap" technique when assessed for quality, time and cost [2]. In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxx ear procedure, one of several ways to change ear projection.
Published work on the technique consists largely of retrospective surgical series, technique modifications and a small number of quality-of-life and complication studies, described below.
infobox: Create the antihelical fold to set back prominent ears [1]

paras: Otoplasty techniques are divided into groups; the Mustardé method sits among those that preserve cartilage and use sutures to change ear projection [1]. It is contrasted with the Merck stitch method, a closed minimally invasive approach that avoids exposing cartilage or removing skin [1]. Other approaches described in the literature include a cartilage-splitting technique that uses neither stitches nor rasping [3], and a vertical mattress suture design described as "tension band fixation" in a series of 104 patients [4].

In prominent ears the antihelical fold is often flattened or absent, so the rim and upper ear project outward. Mustardé's contribution was to recreate that fold with a row of horizontal mattress sutures placed through the cartilage, rather than by scoring or cutting it. Surgery may be combined with other steps such as reducing the concha or repositioning the earlobe, which the wider otoplasty literature describes as part of the same family of procedures [1].

Ear reconstruction has a long history; the Wikipedia otoplasty article records descriptions in the Sushruta Samhita, an 1845 approach to prominent ears by Dieffenbach, and an ear pinback by Edward Talbott Ely in 1881 [1]. Cartilage-cutting methods were developed by Converse and Stenström, Furnas described concha-mastoid sutures in 1968, and Mustardé published his suture technique in 1963 [1][1]. Later developments include Fritsch's incisionless approach and the Merck stitch method [1].

Anesthesia is local, local with sedation, or general, the last being common in children [1]. Operating time in a general overview is given as roughly 1.5 to 5 hours, and the surgery may be outpatient [1]. In a University of British Columbia series of Mustardé otoplasties the median operating time was 95 minutes overall, 48 minutes for one ear and 93 minutes for both [5].

Dressings are typically worn for several days, followed by a snug headband worn during sleep for around 3 to 6 weeks, with bruising and swelling subsiding within about two weeks according to the general overview [1].

General references note that very prominent ears may be corrected from around age 4, with surgery around age 5 to 6 also cited because the ear is nearly adult size by then. In newborns, ear molding is an alternative while cartilage remains malleable [1][1].

Variants include temporary contouring sutures [6], an antihelix instrument-guided folding technique [7], and adding auricular transverse muscle shortening to a perichondrium-sparing approach [8]. An experimental rabbit study examined cartilage changes after carbon dioxide laser-assisted Mustardé otoplasty [9].

Reported complications include hematoma that may need drainage, infection including perichondritis, suture extrusion with granulomas, and overcorrection or unnatural contours, which a general reference calls the most common significant complication [1]. A paper on scarring after Mustardé otoplasty stresses post-operative follow-up [10]. A comparative review of 207 otoplasty procedures in 119 children examined complication rates across techniques [11].

Evidence is largely retrospective. A 2020 single-surgeon study from the University of British Columbia reviewed 119 ears in 68 patients under 18 over about nine years, using an "iron triangle" of quality, time and cost. Twenty of 119 ears (about 17 percent) had suture extrusion, most removed in the office; there was one hematoma and one suture abscess, and two reoperations (1.7 percent). Surgeon and patient satisfaction were recorded for 97 percent of ears with scores. The authors attributed their extrusion rate partly to long follow-up and nonabsorbable nylon sutures, and noted the lack of a control group and unvalidated satisfaction scores [5][2].

A 104-patient series using vertical mattress sutures reported three recurrences within two months, one overfolded antihelix and three suture exposures, with follow-up of three months to two years [4]. A 2018 Adelaide review compared techniques across 207 procedures in 119 children [11]. A 2026 paper examined quality of life after Mustardé otoplasty [12]. The Wikipedia article on otoplasty notes that its own evidence base for the technique is limited, resting on textbooks, older papers and a small angle study [1].
